limits_note: 120 core-hours is the number that binds. At the 2-core default it is 60 hours a month, which is 2 hours a day; at 4 cores it is 30 hours a month, which is 1 hour a day. The 12-hour maximum lifetime per session and the 30-minute default idle stop are what keep the quota from being burned in one sitting.
reliability_note: a codespace stops on an account-level idle timeout (30 minutes by default, settable between 5 and 240 minutes) and is deleted 30 days after it is stopped, irrespective of unpushed changes

free_tier.stated: Quoted: 'All GitHub personal accounts include a quota of free compute time and storage for GitHub Codespaces.' The table row is '| GitHub Free for personal accounts | 15 GB-month | 120 hrs |'. The 120 is a core-hour: the compute column is multiplied by the machine's core count, so 120 core-hours is 60 wall-clock hours on the 2-core default. Quoted: 'The compute cost is proportional to the number of processor cores in the machine type you choose for your codespace, as shown in the following table. For example, the compute cost of using a codespace for an hour on a 16-core machine is eight times greater than a 2-core machine.'
free_tier.notes: The vendor's own header for the column is 'Compute time per month' and the value is 120 hrs, but the included-usage multiplier makes it core-hours. 120 core-hours / 2 cores = 60 hours of the default machine.

retention.stated: Quoted: 'Inactive codespaces are automatically deleted. You can choose how long your stopped codespaces are retained, up to a maximum of 30 days.' and 'By default, GitHub Codespaces are automatically deleted after they have been stopped and have remained inactive for 30 days.' and 'Automatic deletion happens irrespective of whether a codespace contains unpushed changes.' The disk persists across a stop and start until that clock runs out.
retention.notes: The clock runs from the moment the codespace is stopped and restarts when it is connected to again.

egress.terms: no egress allowance or per-byte price published on any page read; the billing page prices compute per core-hour and storage per GB-month and says nothing about transfer

limits.value: 120 core-hours of compute a month on GitHub Free, which is 60 wall-clock hours on the 2-core default machine and 30 hours on a 4-core

Quoted: 'A codespace will stop running after a period of inactivity. By default this period is 30 minutes' and 'Regardless of your idle timeout setting, a codespace has a maximum lifetime of 12 hours.'
Quoted: 'By default, GitHub Codespaces are automatically deleted after they have been stopped and have remained inactive for 30 days.' Automatic deletion happens irrespective of unpushed changes.
Quoted: 'If your account does not have a valid payment method on file, usage is blocked once you use up your quota.' A card is the price of continuity past the quota, not of entry.

The terms scope the machine away from serving. Quoted: 'Any activity that places a burden on our servers, where that burden is disproportionate to the benefits provided to users (for example, don't use Codespaces as a content delivery network, as part of a serverless application, or to host any kind of production-facing application)'.

identity_cost.detail: a GitHub account and nothing else: no card, no phone and no identity document to create a codespace. No hold exists because no card is taken. The gate is at the quota, not at signup: 'If your account does not have a valid payment method on file, usage is blocked once you use up your quota.' Debit acceptance is not stated on any page read.

notes: The core-hour unit is the trap: 120 reads like hours and is not, because it is spent per core, so the wall-clock allowance halves at 4 cores and quarters at 8. The shape is quoted from the overview page as the bottom of the machine-type range: 2 cores, 8 GB RAM, 32 GB storage, and the vendor writes decimal GB, kept unconverted. Identity is email, not card: the gate is at the quota, so a reader who plans one month never meets a card and a reader who plans a second month does. Two things this record does not establish. First, the egress term: no page read publishes a quota, a shaping tier or a price for transfer, so the field is a dash and not 'unlimited'.

shape.note: the 2-core default, quoted as 'from 2 cores, 8 GB RAM, and 32 GB storage'. The vendor writes decimal GB; the numbers are kept unconverted, so 8 GB is about 7.5 GiB and 32 GB about 29.8 GiB.

session_cap.note: 12 hours maximum lifetime per session regardless of settings; stops after 30 minutes idle by default, settable between 5 and 240 minutes; deleted 30 days after being stopped. The disk survives a stop and start.

network_out.ports: forwarded ports get a URL; a port can be made public, so this is the one GitHub free machine that can serve a request

extras.price_arithmetic: 120 core-hours / 2 cores = 60 wall-clock hours a month at USD 0.00 inside the quota. 10 h a day x 30 = 300 h needs 600 core-hours, five times the quota. 24/7 x 30 = 730 h needs 1,460 core-hours, twelve times the quota. Past the quota the rate is USD 0.18 per core-hour, so 600 core-hours would be USD 108.00 and 1,460 core-hours USD 262.80, both of which need a payment method on file.
extras.price_basis: 10 h/day x 30 = 300 h; 24/7 x 30 = 730 h; core-hours, not wall-clock hours
extras.shape_note: vendor states 32 GB (decimal) storage; kept as stated. RAM 8 GB is the vendor's own figure.
extras.unattended_mechanism: a codespace keeps running while the browser is closed, subject to the account's idle-stop timeout; a background process survives until the codespace stops
extras.units: RAM and disk are the vendor's decimal GB, kept unconverted in ram_gib and disk_gib so 8 GB reads as 8 and 32 GB reads as 32. The true values are about 7.5 GiB and 29.8 GiB.

concurrency.note: not published on any page read: the number of codespaces one account may run at once is not stated. What is stated is that the quota is spent per core-hour, so running two 2-core codespaces spends it twice as fast.
